At least that was what he believed. But who could know? ... No. There had been nothing beyond that. Vanity had made him spare her. His show of goodness had been hypocrisy. He had experimented with self-denial merely out of curiosity. He understood that now.

But the murder—would it pursue him for the rest of his life? Must he always carry the weight of his past? Was he actually going to confess? Never. Only one piece of evidence remained against him: the portrait itself. That was evidence. He would destroy it. Why had he held on to it for so long? Once he had enjoyed watching it change and grow old. Lately it had given him no pleasure at all. It kept him awake through the night. Whenever he went away, he was terrified that someone else might see it. It had cast sadness over his passions. Simply remembering it had spoiled so many happy moments. It had acted as his conscience. Yes, it had been his conscience. He would destroy it.

Looking around, he saw the knife that had stabbed Basil Hallward. He had cleaned it again and again until not a stain remained. It shone, bright and gleaming. Just as it had killed the painter, it would kill the painter’s work and everything the work represented. It would kill his past; once that was dead, he would be free. It would kill this monstrous life of his soul, and without its hideous warnings he would find peace. He snatched up the knife and drove it into the picture.

A scream rang out, followed by a crash. The agony in the scream was so terrible that the servants woke in fear and crept from their rooms. Two gentlemen passing through the square below stopped and looked up at the large house. They continued until they found a policeman, then brought him back. He rang the bell several times, but no one answered. Apart from a light in an upper window, the entire house was dark. After a while he withdrew to a neighbouring portico and stood watching.

‘Whose house is that, Constable?’ asked the older gentleman.

‘Mr. Dorian Gray’s, sir,’ the policeman replied.

As the two men walked away, they exchanged a sneering look. One was Sir Henry Ashton’s uncle.

Inside, in the servants’ quarters, the half-dressed staff spoke to one another in hushed whispers. Old Mrs. Leaf wept and wrung her hands. Francis was deathly pale.

After roughly fifteen minutes, he gathered the coachman and one of the footmen and crept upstairs.

Nothing Emma later learned made her change her poor opinion of Mrs. Elton. Her first observations had been fairly accurate. At every meeting, Mrs. Elton seemed just as she had at their second encounter: self-important, pushy, too familiar, ignorant, and badly mannered. She had some beauty and a few accomplishments, but so little sense that she imagined her superior knowledge of the world would brighten and improve a country neighbourhood. She also believed that, as Miss Hawkins, she had occupied a social position surpassed only by the importance she now enjoyed as Mrs. Elton.

There was no reason to think Mr. Elton disagreed with his wife. He seemed proud of her as well as happy with her. His manner suggested he was congratulating himself on bringing Highbury a woman whom even Miss Woodhouse could not equal. Most of their new acquaintances were quite satisfied with her. Some were inclined to praise, others were unused to judging people for themselves; some followed Miss Bates’s kindly example, while others simply assumed the bride was as clever and agreeable as she claimed. Praise of Mrs. Elton therefore spread from person to person, as praise of a bride should, without any obstruction from Miss Woodhouse. Emma willingly repeated her first contribution, speaking pleasantly of Mrs. Elton as ‘very agreeable and very elegantly dressed.’

In one way, Mrs. Elton became even worse than she had first appeared: her feelings toward Emma changed. Probably offended by Emma’s lack of enthusiasm for her offers of friendship, she withdrew in turn, gradually becoming colder and more distant. Emma welcomed the result, but the hostility behind it naturally increased her dislike. Mrs. Elton’s behaviour toward Harriet was also unpleasant, as was her husband’s. They sneered at her and ignored her. Emma hoped this would quickly cure Harriet of her feelings for him, but the emotions that prompted such behaviour lowered both of them greatly in her opinion. There could be little doubt that he had shared poor Harriet’s attachment with his wife as part of their marital confidences. He had probably described Emma’s involvement too, presenting it in the worst possible light for her and the most flattering light for himself. Naturally, they both disliked her. Whenever conversation failed, they could always fall back on criticizing Miss Woodhouse. Since they dared not show their hostility by openly disrespecting her, they expressed it more freely by treating Harriet with contempt.

Mrs. Elton had taken a strong liking to Jane Fairfax from the very beginning. It had started before her quarrel with one young woman could have made the other more attractive. And ordinary, reasonable admiration was not enough: without being asked, without any reason or right to interfere, she insisted on helping Jane and becoming her friend. Before Emma lost her confidence, at about their third meeting, she heard all about Mrs. Elton’s plans to come to Jane’s rescue.

For that reason, I decided to get off as soon as we entered the town and move beyond his hearing. I carried out the plan successfully. My small travelling bag was in the luggage compartment beneath my feet; I only had to turn a hinge to retrieve it. I dropped it down ahead of me, climbed down after it, and was left beside the first lamp, on the first stones of the town pavement. The convicts continued with the coach, and I knew where they would be whisked away to the river. In my imagination I saw the boat and its convict crew waiting at the slime-washed steps. I heard again the harsh ‘Pull away, you!’ delivered as though to dogs, and saw once more that wicked Noah’s Ark lying out on the black water.

I could not have explained what frightened me, since my fear was entirely vague and undefined, but it gripped me powerfully. Walking toward the hotel, I trembled with a dread far greater than the simple prospect of an upsetting or unpleasant recognition. I am certain it never took any clear form. For a few minutes, the terror of my childhood had come alive again.

The coffee room at the Blue Boar was empty. I had ordered dinner and even sat down to eat before the waiter recognized me. Once he had apologized for his failure to remember, he asked whether he should send the boot boy to fetch Mr. Pumblechook.

‘No,’ I said. ‘Certainly not.’

The waiter—the same one who had delivered the travelling salesmen’s Great Protest on the day I became an apprentice—looked surprised. At the first opportunity he placed a dirty old local newspaper so directly in front of me that I picked it up and read the following paragraph:

Our readers will learn with some interest, concerning the recent, almost romantic improvement in the fortunes of a young ironworker from this neighbourhood—what a subject, incidentally, for the magical pen of our not yet universally appreciated fellow townsman TOOBY, the poet of these pages!—that this young man’s first benefactor, companion, and friend was a highly respected individual with some connection to the grain and seed business, whose exceptionally convenient and spacious commercial premises stand within a hundred miles of the High Street. We cannot claim to be entirely free of personal feeling when we record HIM as the Mentor to our young Telemachus. It is gratifying to know that our own town produced the man who laid the foundations of the latter’s fortune.
